name: Tongue posture for voice

lead: Tongue posture for voice is the idea that holding the tongue against the roof of the mouth, as in mewing, changes vocal resonance. It extends the mewing trend, which is aimed at jaw and facial structure, to the sound of the voice.

Proponents propose that resulting changes in oral structure alter resonance. Voice science does recognise that tongue position shapes vocal tract resonance during speech, but no study has tested sustained resting tongue posture as a way to change a person's voice. Mewing itself is described by Wikipedia as an unproven form of oral posture training, and the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence it improves the jaw.

paras: People rest the full tongue against the palate through the day, as in mewing, and listen for changes in their voice. It is usually practised alongside general mewing and posture habits.
The posture itself is not reported as harmful in the sources reviewed. Mewing's main proponent faced a misconduct finding over child patients.

angle.text: Communities extend mewing to the voice, proposing that holding the tongue against the palate changes vocal resonance. Tongue position does shape resonance during speech, though no study tests resting posture for voice change.

lead: Tongue posture for voice is the idea, circulated in looksmaxxing communities, that holding the tongue against the roof of the mouth, as in "mewing", changes vocal resonance. It extends the mewing claim, which concerns jaw and facial structure, to the sound of the voice.[1]

Mewing is described by Wikipedia as an unproven form of oral posture training; professional bodies including the American Association of Orthodontists state there is no evidence it improves the jaw.[1] The same article does not mention claims about voice or resonance.[1] Voice science does recognise that tongue position shapes vocal tract resonance during speech, but no study was found testing sustained resting tongue posture as a way to change a person's voice.

paras: Practitioners rest the tongue against the palate as a habit. Proponents of mewing say sustained tongue pressure reshapes jaws and face; the voice claim is that the resulting oral and facial structure alters resonance.[1]

The orthotropics practice was developed by British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike.[1] The Wikipedia article reports that no credible research has proven orthotropics effective, that most orthodontists do not see mewing as an alternative to jaw surgery, and that Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[1] Interest rose from 2019, driven by social media and associated with looksmaxxing subcultures.[1]
